newsitem.title: PERU: Entrepreneurs pounce on Peru siege.
newsitem.headline: Entrepreneurs pounce on Peru siege.

text.p: The drama at the Japanese embassy residence, where Marxist rebels are holding 105 hostages, has attracted a swarm of small entrepreneurs hoping to make money off the media circus that has descended on the siege site.
"Cigarettes. I've got Hamilton, Marlboro, Belmont," bellows Manuel Corrales, 14, as he circles the cordoned-off compound.

Sleeping alongside the journalists for the eight nights since Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas stormed the luxury residence last Tuesday, Corrales is the only one not looking for a front-page exclusive.
He concentrates his energy on using sign language and a ready smile to commmunicate to the world's media his elevated prices. "Even the Japanese understand me," says the teenager proudly.

The hostage drama has also brought prostitutes to the leafy, middle-class district of San Isidro. "Hi honey, aren't you hot?" is the familiar introduction of prostitute "Sofia" despite the obvious night cold.
The cool Lima climate has not deterred Alberto la Torre from selling his goods. He applies quirky logic to persuade clients that his ice-creams help "fight cold with cold".
The street-hawkers, however, are not the only entrepreneurs taking advantage of new business.
Lima's highly competitive telecommunications companies wasted no time erecting telephone cabins to capture the business of the journalists reporting the unfolding drama.
"When I got here there was one, single phone. I've never seen them install phones so quickly. If only they'd do the same at my house," Peruvian journalist, Juan Vela, said.
But some local shops -- conscious of the havoc wreaked on neighbouring houses by the marauding press -- have refrained from opening to the lucrative new trade.
"We are still working. It is just that we won't work here. We are taking our stuff to another branch," said one cakemaker, as he carried off his wares.
